title: Difference Arrays
summary: The inverse of a prefix sum: applying any number of range increments in O(1) each, then materializing the final array with a single prefix-sum pass.

slides.markdown:
A [prefix sum](prefix-sums) makes range **queries** O(1) after an O(n) build. A **difference array** solves the mirror problem: it makes range **updates** O(1) each, deferring all the actual work to a single O(n) reconstruction pass at the end.

The trade only pays off under one condition — you apply a batch of updates first, then read the final array once. If you need to read the array *between* updates, this technique doesn't apply as-is. That condition is exactly what makes it fast: point edits now, one summation later.

slides.subTitle: diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1]
slides.markdown:
For an array `arr`, its difference array holds the change from each element to the next:

```
diff[0] = arr[0]
diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1]   for i > 0
```

For `arr = [5, 5, 5, 8, 8, 3]`, `diff = [5, 0, 0, 3, 0, -5]` — zero everywhere the array doesn't change, and a nonzero entry exactly where a run of one value ends and another begins. This is exactly the inverse operation of building a prefix sum: prefix sums accumulate, difference arrays record the deltas between consecutive elements.

slides.subTitle: +v at diff[l], -v at diff[r+1]
slides.markdown:
To add `v` to every element in range `[l, r]` (inclusive), touch only two positions in the difference array:

```
diff[l]   += v
diff[r+1] -= v   (if r+1 is within bounds)
```

Why this works: once you reconstruct the real array by running a prefix sum over `diff`, the `+v` at index l means every position from l onward picks up the extra v — because a prefix sum carries every earlier value forward. The `-v` at `r+1` cancels that extra v back out starting exactly one past r, so positions after r are unaffected. Two point writes now stand in for what would otherwise be a loop over the whole range.

The picture to hold: a range update that would take O(r-l+1) time to apply directly collapses into exactly two array writes, regardless of how wide the range is.

slides.subTitle: One prefix-sum pass
slides.markdown:
After applying every range update as a pair of point edits, the difference array holds a record of all the *changes*, not the final values. Materializing the real array is exactly a prefix-sum reconstruction: `result[0] = diff[0]`, then `result[i] = result[i-1] + diff[i]` for each following index.

Each accumulated `+v`/`-v` pair contributes to every index between its two marks and nowhere else, so a single O(n) prefix-sum pass correctly folds in every update that was ever applied — no matter how many updates there were.

slides.sectionTitle: Applying k updates, then reading back
slides.markdown:
```python
def apply_range_updates(n, updates):
    # updates: list of (l, r, v) meaning "add v to arr[l..r]"
    diff = [0] * (n + 1)          # one extra slot so r+1 == n is always valid
    for l, r, v in updates:
        diff[l] += v
        diff[r + 1] -= v

    result = [0] * n
    result[0] = diff[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        result[i] = result[i - 1] + diff[i]
    return result
```

Applying k updates is O(k) total, two writes each. The final reconstruction is one O(n) pass. Total cost: **O(n + k)** — versus O(n·k) for applying each update by looping over its range directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Naive per-update loop vs difference array
slides.markdown:
| Approach | Cost per update | Cost for k updates on size n |
|---|---|---|
| Naive: loop over `[l, r]` and add v to each | O(r - l + 1) | up to O(n·k) |
| Difference array: two point writes, reconstruct once | O(1) | O(n + k) |

The naive approach's worst case is every update spanning nearly the whole array — k updates each touching ~n elements is O(n·k), which degrades badly as k grows. The difference array's cost doesn't depend on how wide any individual update's range is, only on how many updates there are.

The single most common bug: writing `diff[l] += v` and stopping there, without the matching `diff[r+1] -= v`.

Without the cancellation, the prefix-sum reconstruction carries the `+v` forward **forever** — every index from l to the end of the array picks up the increment, not just up through r. The update silently leaks past its intended range, and the bug won't show up as a crash; it shows up as values past r being subtly wrong, which is much harder to notice in a test than an exception would be.

Every range update needs both writes, always as a pair — there's no valid difference-array update that's only one point-edit.

If a range update's `r` is the last valid index (`n-1`), then `r+1` equals `n` — one past the end of an array sized exactly n. Writing `diff[r+1] -= v` there is an out-of-bounds write unless you planned for it.

The standard fix is sizing the difference array as `n+1` from the start (as in the code above), so index n always exists as a safe, unused-in-the-final-result slot to absorb the cancellation. Skipping this sizing and then guarding every write with an `if r+1 < n` conditional works too, but is one more place to forget the check — allocating one extra slot up front removes the branch entirely, the same sentinel-slot trick used for the l=0 boundary in prefix sums.

The same idea extends to range updates over a 2D sub-rectangle, mirroring the 2D prefix sum's inclusion-exclusion but in reverse. To add v to every cell in rows `[r1, r2]` and columns `[c1, c2]`:

```
diff[r1][c1]     += v
diff[r1][c2+1]   -= v
diff[r2+1][c1]   -= v
diff[r2+1][c2+1] += v
```

Four point writes instead of two, because a rectangle has two dimensions of boundary to cancel. Reconstructing the final matrix takes a 2D prefix-sum pass afterward — first over rows, then over columns (or one combined pass accumulating both directions), turning k rectangle updates plus one O(rows·cols) reconstruction into a total far cheaper than updating every cell in every rectangle directly.

slides.sectionTitle: The condition that makes this work
slides.subTitle: Batch first, read once
slides.markdown:
The O(1)-per-update claim has a load-bearing assumption: **you're not reading the array in between updates.** If a caller needs the true current value of some index after every single update — not just at the end — a difference array doesn't help, because the value at any index isn't materialized until the prefix-sum reconstruction runs.

This is the real-world shape of the technique: it's the right tool for "apply a batch of range operations, then report the final result" — a scheduling system applying many interval-based capacity changes before computing final availability, or a calendar tool folding in many date-range adjustments before rendering a view. It's the wrong tool for a system that needs an up-to-date point value after every write, which instead calls for a structure built for interleaved updates and queries, like a Fenwick tree or segment tree with range-update support.

Naming this trade-off explicitly — "this only pays off if reads are batched at the end" — is what separates knowing the mechanism from knowing when it actually applies.

slides.sectionTitle: Prefix sums and difference arrays are inverses
slides.markdown:
It's worth holding both techniques side by side, because they're literally inverse operations on the same idea:

- A [prefix sum](prefix-sums) turns point values into fast range **reads**: build once (O(n)), query in O(1).
- A difference array turns range **writes** into fast point edits: update in O(1), materialize with one O(n) prefix-sum pass.

Building a difference array from an array is the same operation, run backwards, as building a prefix sum from a difference array — each undoes the other. Recognizing which one a problem needs comes down to one question: is the workload read-heavy over a fixed array, or write-heavy with a single read at the end?
